chunks.title: TopicTrail, a memory for what you browse
chunks.text: TopicTrail, a memory for what you browse (featured project). Keeps the content you actually engaged with and finds it again through a RAG pipeline: keyword search plus semantic search over vector embeddings. Status: Bachelor project · in progress · due Jan 2027. Engagement threshold: 0.1 (Design parameter from the PRD). First, opt-in capture: Local. Technologies: RAG pipeline, Embeddings, TDD.

chunks.title: TopicTrail: Solution
chunks.text: TopicTrail. A memory for what you browse: it keeps the pages you actually engaged with and finds them again by meaning, not only by keyword. The planned pipeline. Planned: capture is local-first and opt-in. Only pages you engaged with past an engagement threshold are kept (0.1 in the current design). Planned: retrieval is a RAG pipeline that combines keyword search with semantic search over vector embeddings, so a half-remembered idea still finds the page.

Habib's role: Built solo. Trip search p95: 96 ms (At 300 virtual users, in a k6 ramp to 1,500). Commits, built solo: 387. Technologies: Kotlin MP, SwiftUI, NestJS, LangGraph, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot. Code: https://github.com/Habibwasi/HOP-KMP.

chunks.title: Ridly: My role
chunks.text: Ridly. What I built. I built Ridly alone: the shared Kotlin Multiplatform module, the Android app, the iOS app and the NestJS API. All 387 commits in the repository are mine.

chunks.title: Ridly: AI in the build
chunks.text: Ridly. AI in the build. Planning ran through my LangGraph workflow (AI_Workflow_Global). Agents draft each spec, and a human-in-the-loop gate stops at every step until I approve it or send it back. Claude Code and GitHub Copilot wrote code against rules kept in the repository. Agent.md records the architecture decisions and the verified library versions, and tells the agent to stop and ask when a request conflicts with them instead of inventing a change. A bug-audit skill gives Copilot a checklist of Ridly's own failure modes, such as missing Koin registrations, ViewModel idempotency guards and how money is displayed.

chunks.title: Ridly: Solution
chunks.text: Ridly. A carpooling app for Denmark: drivers post trips, passengers book seats, and both chat in real time, on Android and iOS from one Kotlin codebase. From empty seat to settled trip. Drivers post a trip and review its price. Passengers search by route and date, book a seat, and chat with the driver in real time before the ride. Saved search alerts tell passengers when a matching trip appears. After the ride, the passenger pays the driver directly with MobilePay, and the app tracks each settlement until it is marked as paid. Driver and passenger rate each other, and drivers get a dashboard and a downloadable report of what they earned, for their taxes.

chunks.title: Ridly: Architecture
chunks.text: Ridly. How it fits together. One Kotlin Multiplatform module holds the domain models, the repositories, Ktor networking and the ViewModels, wired with Koin. Android renders them in Compose Multiplatform, and the iOS app wraps the same ViewModels for SwiftUI, so the business logic is written once. The ViewModels follow MVI: the screen sends events, renders an immutable state, and handles one-shot effects such as navigation. The backend is a NestJS 11 API on PostgreSQL through Prisma. Supabase handles sign-in, Socket.IO carries the chat, and BullMQ queues the push notifications. Trip origins and destinations are PostGIS geography points with spatial indexes, which is what trip search runs on. Sentry reports errors from all three apps.

chunks.title: Ridly: Test evidence
chunks.text: Ridly. Proof it holds up. A k6 load test ramped from 300 to 600 to 1,500 virtual users against the API. At the 300-user stage, trip search had a p95 of 96 ms. A second k6 script attacks the API on purpose: missing fields, huge strings, broken tokens, unknown IDs and a burst of 50 requests a second on search. It fails if a single request gets a server error. CI runs the shared module's unit tests and builds both the Android and the iOS app on every push to main and every pull request into it.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: My role
chunks.text: Validation Portal. What I built. All 111 commits in the repository are mine.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: Solution
chunks.text: Validation Portal. A research tool for founders: surveys, customer interviews and an LLM verdict, so they test an idea before they build it. From hunch to verdict. Founders write their assumptions as hypotheses ("I believe [customer] has [problem] and will pay [price] for [solution]"), share a public survey, and log customer interviews with pain scores, quotes and tags. An LLM reads the aggregated numbers and up to 15 quotes, then returns a verdict with themes, key quotes, next steps and a call on each hypothesis. The verdict follows fixed rules: a strong signal needs at least five interviews, 70% pain and 60% concept interest. Anyone can try it as a guest without signing up. Guest accounts and their data are deleted after seven days.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: Architecture
chunks.text: Validation Portal. How it fits together. A React 19 single-page app (Vite, TypeScript) talks to Supabase: PostgreSQL with row-level security on every table, so each user, guest or not, only reads their own data. The AI calls run in Vercel serverless functions. They check the Supabase session before calling GPT-OSS 20B (openai/gpt-oss-20b) on Groq, so the API key never reaches the browser and anonymous traffic can't spend the quota. Resend emails the owner on each survey response, and Cloudflare Turnstile guards every sign-in, sign-up and guest session.

chunks.text: Validation Portal. Proof it works. Validation Portal has no automated tests or CI yet. The evidence is the live demo, which anyone can use as a guest, plus the demo video and the diagrams above.

chunks.title: How this guide works
chunks.text: The assistant in the corner is a small retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over this site. It answers only from the site's own text, cites where each answer comes from, and says "I don't know" when nothing fits. Build step, Chunk: At build time, every case study section, project, the intro, availability, QA record and this page become one chunk each. Missing content is skipped, never indexed. Build step, Embed: Each chunk is embedded with gte-small, a 384-dimension open model that runs locally through Transformers.js. No embedding API. Build step, Ship: Chunks and vectors are written to a JSON file in the repository, so the index always deploys with the content it was built from. Request step, Limit: Each visitor gets 10 questions per 10 minutes, and the whole site 300 a day, to stay inside the Groq free tier. Request step, Embed: The question is embedded with the same model, inside the serverless function. Request step, Retrieve: Keyword search (BM25) and vector search (cosine) each rank the chunks; reciprocal rank fusion merges them, and the top 4 become the sources. Request step, Generate: GPT-OSS 120B on Groq answers in a few sentences, only from the numbered sources, and cites them. Request step, Cite: Source links come from the chunks themselves, never from the model's text. If no chunk shares a keyword with the question and none is close in meaning, the model isn't called at all; the guide says "I don't know". When sources are found but don't answer the question, the model is told to say "I don't know" too. GPT-OSS 120B (openai/gpt-oss-120b) on Groq, with low reasoning effort and a short answer limit. The model ID is one value in the code, so swapping it is a one-line change. About 20 recruiter questions run against the real route every night: the expected source must be retrieved, the answer must cite a source and contain the key facts, and out-of-scope questions must get "I don't know". A few answers are checked for faithfulness by a second model call. A few dozen chunks fit easily in memory, so there is no vector database. With many more documents, the same index format would move to Postgres with pgvector.
